                                SAVE THE LAMPASAS’S INITIAL BRIEF
            Pursuant to State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) Order Nos. 6 and 32, Save

   the Lampasas1 timely files this Initial Brief on June 19, 2026 and urges the Honorable

   Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) and the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission or

   PUC) to approve a route that crosses the Colorado River at the southernmost proposed crossing

   and avoids fragmentation of the Lampasas River Valley, such as Route 296 or route 572 above

   other routes proposed in this proceeding.


                                              I.    INTRODUCTION

           Save the Lampasas does not support the opinion expressed by the Joint Applicants that

   Route 894 best meets the routing criteria in Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.056 and

   16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101(b)(3)(B). Other intervening parties have advocated

   that other routes, including Routes 296 and 572, best address the routing criteria found in

   Commission rules and PURA. Some of these routes were filed with the Application, and others



           1
             Save the Lampasas is an aligned group of intervenors representing more than 50 noticed affected property
   owners and over 550 interested members of the community participating as Save the Lampasas 25, Inc.
                                                                                                    Page 3 of 51


are modified routes using links from the Application. These key routes are reflected on the Routes

of Interest map which is part of the evidentiary record in this case.2

        Save the Lampasas opposes Route 894, which the Joint Applicants have identified as the

“best meets” route, because it does not comply with the applicable statutory and regulatory routing

criteria by bisecting an inordinate number of properties through previously undisturbed sensitive

portions of the Study Area, crosses the Colorado River at a previously undisturbed portion of the

river to the detriment of Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) Colorado Bend State Park

and Post Oak Ridge State Park, unnecessarily negatively impacts the Lampasas River Valley, and

implicates unaddressed engineering constraints, among other concerns. This Initial Brief carefully

analyzes the record evidence and legal precedent which support approval of Route 296 (or Route

572), as the route of interest that best addresses the routing criteria found in 16 TAC

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B) and PURA § 37.056.

        Portions of this study area – particularly the areas of the Colorado River crossing through

the Lampasas River Valley are the subject of Commission precedent.3 This PUC precedent has

taken significant measures to protect new fragmentation of these important Texas Hill Country

regions and should inform the decision in this case.

                                    II.     NEED FOR THE PROJECT

       The Applicants have not established that the timing of the need for this project warrants a

hasty routing process. Texans deserve a thoughtful review of how and when massive infrastructure

corridors that disrupt the undisturbed areas of Texas Hill Country are approved to be taken by

eminent domain and fragmented irreparably.

       The Applicants’ decision to rely solely on ERCOT studies to support the claimed urgent

need for the project is insufficient.4             ERCOT’s determination of need does not involve

consideration of each of the statutory factors that the ALJs and the Commission must weigh in

determining whether or not to grant an application. The Commission (and the ALJs) must weigh

each factor in PURA § 37.056(c) before determining that a proposed project meets the standards

to amend a certificate for public convenience and necessity.5 The evidence in this case shows:

                  The Commission’s obligation to determine if the line is needed for
                  the convenience and necessity of the public is different than the
                  standard of review of need undertaken at ERCOT. The Commission
                  should consider ERCOT’s recommendation, but it is not bound by
                  the results of the ERCOT process. The ERCOT Permian Basin
                  Reliability Plan Study was issued in July of 2024. As I understand
                  to be true in this case, there are changed circumstances from when
                  the ERCOT process and recommendation was issued. 6
       In this case, the Commission at minimum should determine that there is not a level of

urgent need shown for this project that is sufficient to warrant approval of a transmission line route

that inflicts permanent destruction on riparian corridors in the Texas Hill Country.           If the

Commission is unable or unwilling to approve a route that avoids cutting through the middle of a

robust set of routing options that adhere to the applicable routing standards.8

               A.       Record Evidence on Timing

       The Applicants rely solely on the ERCOT Permian Basin Reliability Plan to support the

claimed urgent need for the project.9 However, that Plan shows that, as part of Import Path 2, the

Bell County to Big Hill project is slated to relieve anticipated load needs identified for 12 years

from now in 2038.10 The Applicants provide no analysis of any benefits or specific timing impacts

of this project as an incremental addition to the other 765 kV projects. Each of the other 765 kV

projects involves originating substations that have substantial existing generation tied to those

substations – for example Import Path 1 begins at the “Dinosaur” substation which is in close

proximity to the Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Generation Station.

       In direct testimony filed with the Application, Oncor’s witness Gurley argues that this

proposed line is needed to relieve Generic Transmission Constraints (GTCs) from West to East,

which would allow more renewable power generated in West Texas to get to eastern portions of

the state.11 This post hoc rationalization of describing the project designated as “Import Path 2” as

               B.      Changing Circumstances

       On rebuttal, the Applicants introduce into evidence a portion of the changed circumstances

presents no analysis of the cost of this proposed project versus the potential cost of these

constraints.

       Further, options such as ensuring that data centers have controllable load that could

decrease if certain contingencies occur would also alleviate the concerns about these ERCOT

project.

                                 III.    ROUTING CRITERIA

       A.       Description of Proposed Routes and Joint Applicants’ “Best Meets” Route

       The Application proposes 122 routes for consideration.19 Through this Initial Brief, Save

the Lampasas will demonstrate that, based on the record evidence in this case, the Commission

should approve Routes 296 or 572, or some combination of relevant links of these routes.

However, it is important to note that Save the Lampasas does not oppose an alternate combination

of links in the eastern portion of the study area in Williamson and Bell Counties. A graphical

representation of Routes 296 and 572 (as well as other routes) is shown on Joint Applicants Exhibit

22.

       As further laid out in this brief, because of the nature of the study area selected by

Applicants and the limited routes presented, no route is ideal, and the ALJs and Commission are

left with some untenable choices. If the Commission ultimately determines that approval of this

Application as presented is in the public interest, Routes 296 and 572 come the closest to adhering

to each of the applicable statutory and regulatory criteria by honoring the community values,

environmental, historical and aesthetic impacts of this proposed project in this sensitive portion of

the Texas Hill Country to reduce riparian impacts and bisections of properties in those areas.

       Although all parties sought to develop the record more fully through cross, due to time

constraints those efforts were limited. As such, the ALJs and the Commission must rely heavily

on extensive direct testimony admitted into the evidentiary record in this case. Because this is a

proposed Import project from East to West, this brief will analyze the routes accordingly. This

to the portion of the study that includes alternatives for the Colorado River crossing. A cursory

review of the routing maps reveals what the Applicants confirmed on cross-examination – there

are only 3 routing corridors (or options) in the eastern portion of Burnet County and in the western

portions of the study area.

        In fact, in Burnet County, each of the Routes of Interest converges into one of two nodes

in a very small portion of the map:

       To Link G6

       B.     Analysis of Applicable Routing Factors

       Based on the above, Routes 296 and 572 best address the routing criteria, especially

considering the statutory factors of community values, environmental integrity, impacts to parks

and recreational areas and historical and aesthetics. Save the Lampasas recognizes that no one

route performs best on all routing factors; however, each of the routes discussed above including

Route 572 and Route 296, perform well on the routing criteria in found in 16 TAC §

25.101(b)(3)(B) and PURA § 37.056. Below is a more detailed analysis of the evidence supporting

the routes discussed above and why they are a preferable option to other routes of interest identified

in this proceeding.

                  1.       Community Values

        Community values are a mandatory statutory factor for consideration for the Commission

under PURA § 37.056(c). This generally requires consideration of a “shared appreciation of an

area or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community.”23 As a result,

community values are informed by comments received from members of the public received

during public meetings and can be reflected in the testimony and participation of parties in the

proceeding.24 In this instance the record evidence and Commission precedent help establish key

community values that must be considered in this case.

        The ALJs are aided in this analysis by Commission precedent that has reviewed and

identified key aspects of long-held community values that remain in place today. For example, the

Commission made these findings in a case more than 15 years ago with respect to the Lampasas

River Valley:


       The substantial weigh of evidence in the record demonstrates that the
        communities in the Lampasas River Valley, including Oakalla, Maxdale and
        Ding Gong, have a deep and sustained appreciation of the natural and human
        resources offered by the [Lampasas] river and the surrounding area.25

       The Lampasas River and surrounding areas did not constitute parks or
        recreational areas as those terms were used by URS. However, the significant
        weight of evidence in the record indicates numerous and extensive uses of the
        area for scenic and pleasure drives, hunting, fishing, kayaking, ranching,

Riparian Impacts and Parks
       Landowners in the study area were vocal about the importance of the transmission line

routing avoiding parks and river crossings. The issue was raised in many questionnaires and

comments, was included in landowner testimony, and was a prominent theme throughout the

hearing.

       Texas acquired the land for Post Oak Ridge State Park through voluntary sales, funded by

the Centennial Parks Conservation Fund. 41 Post Oak Falls serves as a central feature of this park.

TPWD recommends that the selected route be setback from the southern boundary of Post Oak

Ridge State Park to protect the viewshed of the headquarters, trailhead, and Post Oak Falls

overlook and to protect the viewshed and use of Colorado Bend State Park.42 The agency identified

the viewshed over the Colorado River Valley from the Parks as a priority for preservation.43

       Route 894 utilizes Link J22 which is located in close proximity to recreational and

protected lands in these two state parks owned by TPWD.44 Many miles of right-of-way associated

with Link J22 falls within the foreground to midground visual zone of park or recreational areas.45

        Habitable structures have evolved to be used as a shorthand by the Commission to also

permanently change the nature and character of private property through government action.109
